utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. We have just a small housekeeping matter. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may be seated, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to remind you that you took -- made a declaration at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. You are still bound by that declaration to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And you still are bound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good. Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will remind you of the request I made at the beginning of your examination. Since we are speaking the same language, we must not overlap, and we both have to take care to make a brief pause between question and answer. In one of your previous answers, you mentioned that near your village there was a pit called Mratunska Jama [phoen]; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Pribilovci mean something to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Pribilovci is a village in Herzegovina where in 1941 Ustashas virtually slaughtered all the residents of the village whom they found there, and I believe that in the 1990s an exhumation was organised from those pits, and the smallest bone extracted was 12 centimeters long, which probably means it belonged to a human fetus. It is a well known fact that Ustashas killed even pregnant expecting mothers. That was not unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see a document from the Prosecution's 65 ter list, number 298. Could we please zoom in on the quadrant next to the right edge in the middle. Can we zoom in along the right edge? That's the middle map, the next one. The one next to it. Further to the right. This is the middle map. I want the one on the extreme right. This one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the top right corner of this map, it says map of the Ustasha genocide against the Serb people on the territory of the NDH independent state of Croatia 1941 to 1945. Can you see that, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: According to the key we see next to the map, these points denote places where killings took place. And along the right edge, we see a key saying that the German envoy, that is Hitler's envoy to the independent state of Croatia, General Edmund Gleise Von Horstenau, otherwise an historian, wrote that Ustashas had killed 750.000 people. The places where the killings took place are marked on this map. Do you know, Witness, whether some representatives of the international community were aware of these facts?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you rightly said, German commanders noted in their reports the monstrosity displayed by the Ustashas in their liquidation of Serbs, and I know that the president of the United States, Theodore Roosevelt, asked that patronage be designated over the Croatian people, because of the crimes they committed in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But that was never established, this supervision?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if you know for what reason President Tudjman as president of the Croatian republic and president of the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union, marked in his platform that one of the objectives of the HDZ was to restore this independent state of Croatia for which the American president Roosevelt asked international guardianship?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is because the attempt to commit genocide and liquidate the Serb people in the Second World War did not succeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have an objection to the question. It is actually a two-part objection. The first is, I don't think this fact is in evidence, that it's marked in the platform that one of the objectives of the HDZ was to restore the independent state of Croatia. Secondly, I don't know how the witness could possibly know the reason President Tudjman did something, that he did or didn't do. The third -- well, I will leave it at that. Two objections is probably enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we did, through the mediation of the OTP precisely, introduce this document -- these documents into evidence. The statute of the HDZ party and the programme objectives of the party that Mr. Tudjman discussed on the 24th of February, 1994, and 1991. In many places in those documents it is noted that the independent state of Croatia is not only a quisling creation and an historical crime, but also an expression of the time honoured aspirations of the Croatian people. And I am asking the witness as a person who lived in Croatia from the Second World War when he was born until 1991 if he's aware of the reasons for including these points in the HDZ programme. I don't think it is baseless.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I think counsel's referring to Exhibit 873 in evidence, which in fact contains the platform and objectives of the HDZ. There is a reference to this quotation which we've heard a lot about from Tudjman, and that -- I'm not going to say anything about that. But that quotation certainly does not support what counsel put to the witness, which was that the -- that one of the objectives of the HDZ was to restore this independent state of Croatia. Whatever -- however objectionable that quotation from Tudjman may have been about what he was saying about the past, that is one thing. But it's something entirely different to say that the objective of the HDZ, that the explicit objective of the HDZ was to restore the independent state of Croatia. I don't think that is contained anywhere in Exhibit 873.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is true that is not explicit in Exhibit 873, but I didn't say that, nor did I ask such a question that Tudjman said it was one of the objectives to restore. I didn't use the word "to restore." I only said -- in fact I asked the witness how he explained the fact that Mr. Tudjman as one of the programme objectives introduces such a creation. It is not to restore, and I did not use the word "to restore."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like to re-read the question, because for starters, I didn't understand it. The question says: "Can you tell me if you know for what reason President Tudjman as president of the Croatian republic and president of the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union ..." Up to that I think everybody knows the answer. He was president because he was elected president. Then you say: "... marked in his platform that one of the objectives" -- I must confess here I don't understand what is meant by the platform here but I see the two of you seem to understand each other about what is meant by that. "Marked in his platform that one of the objectives of the HDZ was to restore ..." Now you say you didn't use that word. It may very well be wrong interpretation. But that is what we see on the transcript. It says: "To restore this independent state of Croatia for which the American president Roosevelt asked international guardianship"; that is how it is stated. If that is not what you said, correct it, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for the effort you invested. I really did not say that word and it would have been a misrepresentation of the text, which is very precise. I said it was one of the programme objectives. The question was asked before, because both the Prosecutor and I, as Defence counsel, insisted on what kind of programme and platform the HDZ had. We have this speech of Mr. Tudjman of the 24th of February, 1990, which was later transformed into their political programme, in which he says that the independent state of Croatia is not only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you have explained sufficiently to say that what I read would have been a misrepresentation. Give us the correct representation. Just tell us now how that question should have read, instead of how it stands now. In other words, put the question to the witness once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, my question is: In your view, why did Mr. Tudjman, speaking primarily as the leader of the HDZ party at their founding convention, introduce one of -- as one of the programme objectives the independent state of Croatia, that was the essence of my question. All this is related to your previous testimony to the effect that President Roosevelt had suggested what he had suggested during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I again object. The question is essentially the same question without the word "restore" in it. But it is essentially the same question that one of the programme objectives is the independent state of Croatia, and if counsel wants to insist on that, I would ask for a reference, what the basis is in Exhibits 873, what he's relying on in that exhibit to put that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, if this question is not contained in that statement, can't the witness just answer and say, no, it is not there or it's there. If he says it is there, then in cross-examination you can take it up with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I mean, that is one way to go, certainly. But I think it's -- I think that counsel is misrepresenting what the evidence is. We have in evidence, the Prosecution put it in evidence what the programme objectives of the HDZ were. It's Exhibit 873. And I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it doesn't say one of them is the independent state of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. It does not say that one of the programme objectives is the independent state of Croatia. It does not say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, does it say so or doesn't it say so? I would like to resolve this, otherwise I am just going to have to rule on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is not written in the programme objectives, nor did I say that. Our problem here is this: The Prosecutor seems to believe that that is what I mean. However, he cannot know what I mean. I asked the witness very specifically: Why, in a speech that later became the programme platform of the party, was it necessary to mention the independent state of Croatia, not only as a quisling creation and a fascist crime, and it was both of these, but also an expression of the historical aspirations of the Croatian people. So Mr. Tudjman says at this Assembly the independent state of Croatia is an expression of the historical aspirations of the Croatian people. And I'm asking the witness why did Tudjman say that. My learned friend is making an objection which is completely inappropriate. It is a completely different matter that the question doesn't suit him, I cannot do anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence counsel has just put a completely different question to the witness and one that I do not object to. Though I'm not sure how the witness is going to be able to say why Tudjman said something, but fine. But the question now, as has been expressed is completely different from formulation number 1 and formulation number 2. This is formulation number 3, and it is quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am mindful of the differences, but I think I am going to rule now, because I think this is a matter that can be dealt with by some other means. Mr. Milovancevic, I will allow the question. I have allowed the question. Just put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you heard the question. Your Honour, shall I repeat the question? Or what I have already said suffice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have asked three versions of the same question. I would like you to put your final version to him and we must all know what it is you are asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will formulate my question in such a way as to avoid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one minute, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us your opinion on this, Witness. Why did Mr. Tudjman, at the founding convention of his party, speaking about the programmed objectives of the HDZ, say about the independent state of Croatia that it was not only a quisling creation and a fascist crime but also an expression of the historical aspirations of the Croatian people? Do you have an opinion about this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that because Croatian parties in the past, starting with Starcevic onwards until Tudjman, all started to create an independent Croatian state. In the period between 1941 and 1945, the independent state of Croatia was created as an expression of the aspirations of the Croatian people, regardless of the crimes committed by Ustashas in World War II. Tudjman believed that this struggle of the Croatian people should be continued in some way in order to create an independent Croatian state. With what means? We'll see that later if we compare what happened to Serbs in 1941-1945 and in the 1990s. We will see that in the 1940s as well Serbs were thrown out of the Croatian constitution as a constituent people. Ethnic cleansing was committed in Western Slavonia in 1941 and in the 1990s in Grubisno Polje, for instance. Serbs were dismissed from their jobs en masse in the 1940s and in the 1990s alike, and almost 400.000 Serbs were forced to leave Croatia in 1990 to 1993. Mainly Serbs from urban communities, whereas Serbs living in villages managed to defend themselves, mainly by force of arms. The same emblems were in play in the 1940s, and in the 1990s the same hymn, the same coat of arms. Serbs are nowhere mentioned as a constituent people, and kuna was reinstated by Tudjman as the currency that existed back in the early 1940s. Tudjman introduced the kuna again. Then we have the language split. In the Vienna agreement of 1850, Croats had accepted the common Serbo-Croat language. Tudjman discontinued this agreement about the common language and proceeded to cleanse the Croat language of what they called borrowings from Serbian, or Serbisms. The result was a new speak that was a little ridiculous even to Croats themselves, but it was rather a successful attempt to cleanse the Croat language of all common words, although it was essentially the same language. And that is not to mention the terror that Serbs were exposed to in the 1990s as they were in the 1940s. Because obviously nobody would leave their home of their own will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what happened to the Serbs who were staying, who were residing in the areas under the protection of the United Nations? In one sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly, for the most part, the United Nations were just observers, so what was happening, because we saw that all attempts of Croatia and of its newly formed army what were aimed at conquering territory under Serb control ended in massacres, starting with that on the Miljevci plateau where were killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, excuse me, Mr. Witness. Let me ask you this question. If it should be necessary, I will ask you specific questions about all these events but I put to you a very short question. How did all of this end?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all ended in the wholesale destruction, the total destruction of all these Serbs settlements and the expulsion of the Serbs from them who were found refuge in Krajina from Ravni Kotari, et cetera, from Lika.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the name is of the operation which ended the combat -- the war operations in that area?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Croatian army's operation, the so-called Storm, Oluja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will suffice. Can you tell us, you mentioned that you were born in a Croatian village. What did you possess of property there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my native village, I had several houses. Each one of my brothers and I myself had a house, and as we had our families as well, we would go there for our holidays, annual vacations, and we built each house there, and our parents also had one. So that we had about five houses in all. We had our vineyards there by the Krka river. It was an idyllic place, very suited for one's vacation. Apart from that, I also had property in Sibenik, and my wife also had a house which she had inherited from her parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened to that property?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My flat was seized as was Mr. Raskovic's immediately when we had to flee, after the petition which was implemented against us. All our effects, all our things, all the furnishings and furniture in the flats were taken, and the houses in the village of Bogatic, after this operation of the Croatian army, that is what completely destroyed, as were all of the houses in the village. The entire village was obliterated. There is not a single house that is habitable there, nor did a single inhabitant return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I will interrupt you. How was the -- this operation called in your village?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My village was at the line of separation, the contiguous line with UNPROFOR. This was the line where there was a zone where there were no operations and there was no reason for the village to be destroyed. As a matter of fact, we helped the Croats who had fled to our village and my father actually put them up in the different vacant houses. They spent there several months under, his, my father's protection and actually they ate up all of our food stores. They shared everything they had, simply speaking, with them, but the food was scant and after a while they left.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will counsel and witness please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the interpreter is asking that you please do not overlap, you and the witness. Will you please give each other a chance. And may you speak slowly, please, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you say that you hosted them, your neighbours or your -- these refugees who had fled the JNA, which is what you said. When was this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was before this operation of the Croatian army directed at the Miljevci plateau, below from where we were. So they were frightened and they fled their houses, which were not destroyed afterwards. And they could and did return to their houses which were habitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Popovic. Was any of your property restituted or compensated for? Can you go back there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no place to go back to, because the flat, not only my flat, about 30.000 flats in Croatian cities have been occupied -- haven't been given to Croats for their use by the state of Croatia, to citizens from both Croatia and from Bosnia who had gone there. And this was done, in fact, in the perfidious manner invoking some law on housing relations which used to be valid during the time of the Socialist Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Whose flats were these? You were referring to 30.000 flats.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were flats given to Serbs for their use as tenants from their work organisations, from where they worked by way of compensation for what they were contributing to their work organisations. They would be given flats or, rather, the right of occupancy to those flats as tenants or would be given credits for building their family houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic. That will do. How did those Serbs come to remain without those flats? What happened did they sell them? Did they give them away?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply speaking, because of the terror which was being -- out against them, people just had to leave. So many people had left their flats and their vacationing houses and cottages along the seaside. Nobody cared about those. Everybody wanted to save their lives and their families and children's lives, and for years nobody was able to return and because of the force inflicted on them by Croatia. And still today people cannot return because Serbs are being subjected to veritable orders as we have witnessed in the vicinity of Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the examination-in-chief is completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Alex Whiting.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm one of the Prosecutors in this case, and I'm going to ask you a few questions. I want to start with the -- something that we ended or that you ended on on Friday, and that is Exhibit 938. I don't believe it's in e-court. I think copies were passed out. And if anybody hasn't brought their copy along, I made more copies. It's this one. Yes. I have some copies. Sir, you remember testifying about this photograph on Friday?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in fact, did I understand correctly that you -- you provided this photograph to Defence counsel during your proofing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you -- during your proofing with the Defence counsel, did you tell Defence counsel, did you tell them the same thing that you told the Trial Chamber here about this photograph on Friday?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified that this came from the book, a book called "The Spiritual Genocide," which was published in 1997. You testified that the photograph, this photograph was a message intended for you. And you even went so far to say that the message intended for you was "quite clear." Do you remember that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do remember, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, when you say this photograph was a message intended for you, are you -- I want to get clear on this -- are you saying that the person who wrote the book included the photograph as a message to you? Or are you saying that the people, whoever spray-painted this on the gate, was trying to send a message to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The message was sent by those who also participated in our expulsion from Sibenik. Because you can see the signature says "the Ustashas from the bank," that is a message addressed to me. And here on the left it says "here lies Jovo." That is a message to some others and probably to his family, because he was already dead. He died in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, sir, just if you could please focus on my question, please. So you're saying that the person or persons who spray-painted this on the gate in 1997 was trying to send a message to you? Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, sir, you conclude that because it says "Ustashas from the bank." And from that you conclude that this spray-painted message is a message for you? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because they are from the bank. The organisation for which and in which I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, it doesn't have -- let's be clear here. It doesn't have the name of your bank on here, does it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is just one bank in Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Was there just one employee? Sir, were you the --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the other --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you the only employee of that bank? Or were there other employees?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this is immediately associated with the name of Jovan Raskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But that's not your name, sir, is it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I am -- it is quite clear that this refers to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can I just ask you a question, please. Because you've told us already that you think it is quite clear that it refers to you. This spray-painted message does contain a name or at least part of a name which you say refers to Jovan Raskovic, right? The Jovo there is --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Jovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, if the person or persons who are spray-painting this message on the gate wanted to send a clear message to you, why didn't they put your name on there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, this message was on the gate. The entrance to the bishop's mansion of the Serbian bishop, and this is where Jovo Raskovic used to park his car, in the yard there. So that particular place was chosen because precisely of that fact and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir. Sir, I'm going to interrupt you, because I don't have a sense that you're focussing on my question. I want you to please listen carefully to my question. If the person or persons who spray-painted this message on the gate wanted to send you a clear message, why didn't they simply put your name there, as they had with Jovan Raskovic? Can you think of any reason why they didn't include your name?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot. Probably there would be no space left for these two Croat, Croatian coat of arms and the U, the letters U and the HDZ. But it was quite clear to them that I would read that message right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But sir, you didn't live in Sibenik at that time, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't. But of course you can have messages sent via intermediaries and probably this priest who came to the parish house --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir -- sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- he actually recorded it. He took a photograph of it, because it was the parish house, the bishop's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you hadn't lived -- this was in 1997, and you hadn't lived in Sibenik for years; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. Yes, but I sent out feelers. I'm always on the look-out to know what is happening. Everything that -- to hear about everything that refers to me, and I have very strong sense developed for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So strong, in fact, that you still insist that this, this photograph, this message refers to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm 100 per cent sure that it did, that it does, because why would they, precisely in my town --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And -- an in association with a bishop.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're 100 per cent sure. So you could not be more sure of this? 100 per cent is as sure as it gets. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, the petition also -- did not have my name on it in all places either, but it was implemented, it was carried out in practice. We were expelled and there were so many people who were expelled who don't have any shred of evidence of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hundreds of thousands of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll talk about that in a moment, sir. But all I'm asking is that you say you're 100 per cent sure that this refers to you. That's your testimony. You're 100 per cent sure that this refers to you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By the way, what is the message that they're trying to communicate to you, in a sentence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can see here "Long live the Ustasha, the NDH." They know that I cannot accept to live in an Ustasha climate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you were living in Belgrade at the time, weren't you, in 1997. So what was the message that was being communicated to you, sir, by this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The message was: Don't return. Don't ever entertain the idea of returning, because I did submit some formal requests for my flat to be restituted to me. However, that remained just dead letter on paper, and probably in order to induce me to abandon the entire idea altogether and not even think about it, that was the idea, because they knew that I was a great champion of human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: All of these things that you have now told us about this photograph, you shared with Defence counsel before you came here and testified; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the way I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no other interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were trained as a lawyer and you worked as a lawyer; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I actually represented at the bank, in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that as a lawyer, being trained as a lawyer and working as a lawyer, that you understand the importance of being precise, of being accurate when you speak?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bed of Procrusteans.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to touch that one. But, sir, you also understand that you're testifying under oath here, right? You realise that, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That is what I said, I believe, at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And all the more reason, if you're testifying under oath, to be particularly precise and careful and accurate in the way you testify; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I am the closest to this here piece of evidence, that I am the one who is the most knowledgeable about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that no one can know the truth about it better than I.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, please, listen to my question. I didn't ask if you were knowledgeable or what you knew. I asked if you understood that being under oath it's particularly important to be precise and careful and accurate in the way you testify. You understand that, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And I do not shirk from it, because I know what is and what is not the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could look, please at Exhibit 880. You looked at this during your direct examination. Sir, you remember looking at this article during your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this article recounts what Ratko Licina said. This article is from August of 1990, and it recounts what Ratko Licina said at the time about events that were occurring. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it accurately records what he was saying at the time, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this is a -- but Ratko Licina was a Serb politician in the Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a deputy of the Serbian Democratic Party to the Croatian Sabor, the Croatian Assembly, and he represented Gracac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this is a Croatian newspaper, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Vjesnik has its seat in Zagreb. It is based in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So this Croatian newspaper in August of 1990 is accurately publishing long quotations from Mr. Licina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was actually the inaugural address of our deputies to the Croatian Assembly which was proved by -- endorsed by the Main Board and their constituency probably. It was not something extemporised, you know. Now we may have to zoom in on what I believe is the third paragraph of the text. And it starts --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You probably have to move to the left. No, the other way. Keep going. And move down. Okay. Let's stop there. Sir, I think -- sir, sir, I don't think you -- I think because he's leaning so close to the earphones I mean to the mics it is causing a feedback.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, do you see --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the text, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you see a sentence, and I'm reading from the third paragraph on the first page in English where it says: "This, Ratko Licina said, which is still happening to the Serbian people in Sibenik, and in Primosten where for two days already they have been gathering signatures for a petition to expel the academy members, Jovan Raskovic, Branko Popovic and Marko Dobrijevic is a fascist expulsion orchestrated by the democratic Croatian leadership." Do you see that sentence, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't see that sentence. The third paragraph, you said? Oh, yes, yes, I see "Ratko Licina." I see the text but not the -- your quotation in the third column. What I see is night refugee columns reminiscent of war, Ratko Licina, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is completely my fault. Could we zoom out a little bit? I have located the exact spot. Maybe Mr. Perovic will help me out on this. Could we go to the next page in the B/C/S. I'm getting assistance from Mr. Black, who always comes through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 2, the third paragraph from the top to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, great. I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the third column, the second paragraph from the top. It starts with the words "this is what Ratko Licina said, what continues to be happening to the Serbian people," something to that effect. So the very top of the third column.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I see it now and I'm very grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, do you see it now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "This, said Ratko Licina."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. It's right in the middle. Okay.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that an accurate description of the petition? A petition to expel the academy members in a fascist expulsion. Is that accurate, what Mr. Licina had said?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, the question is: Is it accurate? Is that an accurate description of the petition?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, by all means. I was in Sibenik during those days and I know. I crossed the central square where this ostracism was being voiced..

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, please, you only need to answer the question, and you fully answered the question when you said "certainly, by all means." Now, in fact, in your direct examination you yourself said that the petition said that you should be expelled from Sibenik. Right? Is that what you say the petition said? That you should be expelled from Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And there is even the text of that petition available.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in which the message is clearly sent by name to Professor Raskovic as the president --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, I will ask you a second time. When one of the lawyers is talking to you says "stop," please do stop, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, so are you saying, then, that the petition demanded or demanded of the authorities that you be expelled from Sibenik? That the authorities -- that the Croatian authorities or the authorities in Sibenik expel you from Sibenik? Is that what the petition demanded?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The message was unequivocal that we were not welcome and that they were very unhappy that we were among them. That's how it was formulated. And they would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would be no end to their happiness if we would simply disappear from their community.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, in that answer, you didn't say the word "expulsion" and I am focussed on the word "expulsion," that Mr. Licina described it as an expulsion, and you described it in your evidence as an expulsion. So did the petition ask for you to be expelled from Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And our names were written there explicitly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at the petition, because you're right, the text of the petition is available. And if we could look, please, at Exhibit 02664917.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You know, I apologise to Defence counsel because I usually send a list of exhibits that I am going to use right as I start the cross-examination and I forgot to do it. I've just done it now. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You mean you've just sent them now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. I usually do it just at the beginning of the cross-examination, and it slipped my mind, so I have just done it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could focus in, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Your opposite number is on his feet. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why did you stand? Maybe you're tired of sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think he was just being polite and saying it is fine, which I appreciate. Thank you. And if we could focus in on the right, the article on the right-hand corner, please. And -- yes, you have to move over to the -- move it all the way to the right, please. Yes. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you able to read that, sir, in the right-hand corner? Or -- we can make it a little bigger, I think.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need, sir. I recognise this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now we've lost it. You have to move all the way to the right. And then to the top, please. There we go. There it is. Thank you. Now, this is an article from Politika and it's dated the 23rd of August, 1990. Now Politika, you told us in your direct examination, right, is a newspaper published in Belgrade which, in fact, you read at the time, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So the text of the petition is reproduced here and it says: "You have offended us and humiliated us deeply, Messrs. Jovan Raskovic, Branko Popovic and Mark Dobrijevic. We shall never forgive you this. We are very sad at these moments and unhappy that you are among us. What is more, we would be happy if you disappeared forever from our environment. Gentlemen, you have not done anything to deserve it." Now, that's the text of the petition, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, sir, whatever the extreme nature of this language is, it does not say anything about expulsion, does it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was placed just a little above that teen sitting at those tables where the citizens were coming to sign the book, that is close to the centre of town. In fact, it is the centre of town, the central square, near the theatre. I think it was quite clear to everybody what they should do when they come there and over 20.000 signatures were in fact collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and now it makes no -- there is no point in trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- relativise this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, please listen to my question. I am trying to be precise and accurate. This petition does not call for you to be -- does not call on the authorities or on anybody to expel you, does it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there can be no dilemma that this referred to us and that we were unwelcome. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the results of this petition, all these books were --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is there a reference to expulsion in this petition, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as we are designated as "unwelcome."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, do you understand the difference between unwelcome and expulsion?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just after that we were invited, in fact I was invited by my manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please, please, I have put a question to you. Do you appreciate the difference between a petition which says you are unwelcome here and a petition which calls for your expulsion? Do you understand -- do you appreciate the difference between those two things? Or do you think those are the same?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you are trying to make me say whether it was some sort of trial. No, it was not a trial where it would be said the decision has been made to expel you, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not trying to get you to say anything. I'm just trying to get you to answer my questions. Okay? Please focus on my questions. The question is: Do you appreciate the difference between a petition which says you are unwelcome here. We would be happy if you weren't here," and a petition which calls for your expulsion? Do you appreciate the difference between those two things, or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know of all kinds of petitions that may exist. I know what plebescite is. I know what --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- referendum is, but this is something unique.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, this is not a question about petitions. This is a question about language. You told us a few minutes ago before I showed you this petition, that the petition asked for you to be expelled from Sibenik. I put that question to you and you said "yes." Now my question is: Do you understand, do you appreciate the difference between a petition which says "you're not welcome here. You're not -- we would be happy if you weren't here" and one that calls for your expulsion? Or do you think those are the same things? It's a simple question, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think from the linguistic point of view it's not the same thing. There is a difference. But in my reality, in the reality for me, the message is unequivocal, because the essence of it was that we were proclaimed persona non grata by the political parties in Sibenik and just after that we were prevented from going back to our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, we'll talk about that --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Raskovic was disallowed from getting into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll talk about that in a moment. But now that you have conceded that there is a difference between expulsion and what is written in this petition, would you agree with me, then, that you were not being precise and accurate and careful in your testimony when you told me that the petition called for your expulsion from Sibenik? Would you agree with me, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not really distinguish between -- all I know is how I felt and what I was subjected to after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, we're talking about --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And whether there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The question is: Would you concede that you were not precise and accurate and careful when you testified earlier that the petition asked for you to be expelled from Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, when an entire people are being expelled the fate of one person means nothing. But if you are trying to question even my expulsion, that is absolutely preposterous, it makes no sense. The pressure was such --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, did you --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was so great not only against me, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand the question that I put to you just now? Were you able to understand the question that I put to you? Or no? Did you not understand it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you answer it, please. Sir, could you please answer it, then, if you understood it. The question is: Would you concede that you were not precise and accurate and careful when you testified earlier and on Friday that the petition asked for you to be expelled from Sibenik? That was not accurate, was it, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still continue to believe and claim that that petition asked for our expulsion. And I think that's the way I understood it. Maybe others can read it differently. At least I understood it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that's not what you testified to, sir. What you testified to is that the petition called for your expulsion, that it said it in the text. And it doesn't say it in the text, does it, sir? It does not call for your expulsion.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, what would have happened with that entire design if my name had not been there? Then I would not be able to prove at all that that had happened to me. But luckily my name does feature there. If my name were not in this document, we could interpret it this way and another, whether it was Branko Popovic, member of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party that was meant. However, there is no dilemma. At any rate, I understood the message the way I understood it, and I don't know how else I could possibly interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- I think this is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is, indeed. We shall take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could this document be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number 939.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I just ask a question, Mr. Whiting? You picked up the last two documents, I thought in support of the points you were making from this Exhibit 938.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It was a completely different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it? Oh, okay. Then I should have interrupted you a little earlier. Can I just check something with the witness, here? With respect to this document Exhibit 938, the picture on that document, Witness, did I understand you correctly to be saying the message refers to you because of the words "Ustasha from the bank"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do they mean to you? What message are they saying to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The message is, as I have said before when answering one of the Prosecutor's questions, that I should not even think of going back, because they always fear that what they've done to us as innocent people will come back to haunt them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me ask my question slightly differently. To whom do the words "Ustasha from the bank" refer, in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's probably the employees of the bank who participated in the creation of that petition, because the pressure that started with the petition continued just a few days later in the bank where I worked, and it was made clear to me that I would no longer be allowed to enter the bank and the director was told to communicate that to me. HDZ militants intended to stop me from going back to my work, in the bank, and that's why my manager invited me to tell me that I had better take some annual leave and leave until things settled down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just wanted to understand who those words referred to. Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now speaking now about the -- again, about the petition from August of 1990, you testified also, did you not, that it had been organised by the HDZ, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Possibly other parties took part in it, too, but the HDZ was the leader. Prior to that, a similar petition targeted Raskovic in particular, in Primosten.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just asking about the petition that we've now seen the text of. Could we look at another document, this is ERN 02664892. And this is an article from another newspaper on the same date, the 23rd of August, 1990 and it's the -- this one is from the newspaper Oslobodjenje. You know that newspaper to be a Bosnian newspaper; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, we have to focus --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you scroll down, please. Okay, that's not the correct page in the e-court. Is that the only page that's in there? No, that's not it either. That's it, okay? Well, I have a hard copy of it. If we could put, with the assistance of the usher, if we could put the hard copy on the ELMO, please, and let's see if the translation is ... Is there an English version of this? Your Honours, on the English screen, do you have a text which says "Sibenik does not want Raskovic"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, Mr. Whiting. We have the other newspaper which you said was the wrong one. That's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just need a moment to catch up here, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the heading of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. The number should be 02664892. Did I give the wrong number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be of assistance. We can see it on the screen in B/C/S, the passage from the text titled "Sibenik does not want Raskovic." However, I cannot be of assistance as regards the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, we've got that Mr. Milovancevic. We're trying to get the English version. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's the English. Can we scroll down on the B/C/S? Or is that -- or actually, go to the second page of the B/C/S. Okay. On B/C/S we have it on the ELMO; and on the English, it is on the e-court. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, this is another article about the petition and it says that it was organised, the decision was brought at a joint party meeting organised on the initiative of HSLS, which stands for the Croatian Social Liberal Party. That's not the HDZ, is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So would you accept that this was in fact organised at the initiative of a different party, at the HSLS party?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see this. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number 940.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, you spoke about harassment that occurred after the petition, but -- and, sir, I'm actually done with that document, so ... If we could lower the ELMO. But, sir, in fact after the petition of the 23rd of August, 1990, you did continue to leave your apartment on occasion, and you went to your work, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, after the petition appeared, the very next morning, as I came to the bank, I noticed that all the employees, starting with the receptionist, are avoiding all contact with me. The receptionist disappeared as soon as I said good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, I'm going to interrupt you because you told us this on direct examination. My question to you was to confirm that in fact you did go back to your bank, after the petition was -- this petition happened; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning I came to the bank, and then the manager invited me to his office to talk. And he told me that a group of employees had been to see him, and that they wanted to prevent me from going into the bank. I think those people who had come to see him were HDZ members. I knew them as HDZ members. So he suggested that the best thing for me to do would be to take a vacation, because I had 16 days of annual leave that I could take, and then after that, we would see what we were going to do when the situation settles down, and I knew the situation would not settle down because the tensions continued --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to increase. On the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions. Did you take the vacation, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After the --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accepted his suggestion and I took the vacation, not of my own will.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, after the vacation was completed, did you return to the bank?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called up. The last day, I called up the manager --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on the 16th day of my leave to tell him I was coming back, and he said: Where are you going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just please answer the question. Did you return to the bank, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I came back, contrary to what the manager wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, sir, this petition occurred in August of 1990 and you continued to be employed by the bank until March of 1991; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did, but I didn't do anything. They took everything away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. I believe you testified on direct examination that you listened to the music that was being played in boom boxes by other employees. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They took away my archives, the law files that I had maintained for 25 years as the bank's legal officer. They also divested me of my license for representation in court. They appointed a different person, a lady assistant of mine, to take over the archival records, and they moved me to another legal office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, so you continued to go to the bank, but you did not -- you did not do any work there is what your testimony is; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was given a new -- actually appointment by decision as if I were a beginner, and they gave me this small office like a little cafe, which was devoid of any furnishing, no books, no nothing. And I sat there for eight months idle, without being assigned any work to do. They were just playing games with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I understand --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably they were counting that I would actually become so exasperated as to leave of my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Please focus on my question and just answer my question, if you would. So, sir, to be clear and precise and accurate, you were not, during that time, put into home detention, were you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could say that I was, because any going out of my house was risky for me --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so that I actually avoided to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you just told us that you went to the bank for eight months. So you were not in home detention, were you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. But later I hardly ever dared go out to town. And if I did, it was something which was a blitz sort of exercise, because I wanted to avoid being harassed in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. But I just want to get clear on the answer to my question. You were -- it's correct to say that you were not put in home detention? That is correct, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a way, yes, there was no court injunction or order of that kind, something of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, please, if you could answer my question directly. You were not put in home detention during that time, right? All of these other things happened, but you were not put in home detention, were you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, actually I'm not quite clear on what kind of home detention you are talking about. Does that require some sort of a document, or is it just my feeling of fear or what have you that will suffice for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, what I mean by "home detention," which I think is a common understanding, is that you were detained in your home. You were not detained in your home, were you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all sorts of things happened every day there. Either in the case of the building where I lived there would be graffiti --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- written that would actually amount to persecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, please focus on my question and answer my question. You were not detained in your home, were you? All of these other things happened; you've described them. But you were not physically detained in your home, were you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any attempt on my part to go out anywhere was associated with some provocations or assaults or people crying out things at me. In our building, they would write --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this is Croatia. Go. You have two daughters. Beware. And things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, you were able to leave your house. You did, in fact, leave your apartment, so you were --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, sir. I was able to go out and I did go out. But I would transact my business very quickly, and I would return very quickly home in order to avoid --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, now --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- being exposed to any such possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now please answer my question. You were not put in home detention, were you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could be understood as some sort of an isolation, because I was not free. I was not free as a citizen to go out. I had problems, wherever I appeared. They punctured our tyres. They harassed us by telephone every half an hour. There was this leaflet --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour I have put this question now about eight times to the witness. I would ask that the Court at this point order the witness to answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I refrained from reacting by raising an objection in the belief that all of these questions would be clarified by the witness's answers. My learned colleague, the Prosecutor, in my view, should have explained to the witness what house detention is. The witness is a jurist but this institution never existed in Yugoslavia. We have prison, imprisonment, we have detention, we have service, serving of a sentence. These are the three institutions which exist in our country, according to the constitution, the law, and jurisprudence. We do not have this institute of house detention. So for heavens sake, I don't understand what kind of a house detention are we talking about? Who is the one that takes a decision on detaining, a house detaining a person? In Yugoslavia and Croatia, in no republic of Yugoslavia, did there exist such an institution as a notion or in practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I have warned you before not to call in God's name in court, and I ask you again to refrain from doing so. I am trying to look for the transcript where the witness did ask Mr. Whiting what home detention was, and Mr. Whiting said that as is understood by everybody, is to be kept in the house. Now, I don't think there has been any suggestion, Mr. Milovancevic, that there was home detention in the legal structure of Croatia or anywhere else. The question is just: You were not kept in home detention? I think it is a simple enough question to answer. You are either -- you were either kept there or you were not kept there. And without asking Mr. Whiting to respond I am going to rule that objection as out of order and overruled. May the witness please answer. I have told you before, if I have ruled, Mr. Milovancevic, and you are not happy with my ruling, it's open to you to take the ruling on appeal. You don't argue with me about it. Now, will you please answer the question and tell us -- to answer the question whether you were kept in home detention or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was not kept in that by some persons. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is the end of the answer. I don't need any more answer. Okay. You've got an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me the first time that you were interviewed by the Defence in this case. And by that I mean either the Defence counsel, or investigators representing the Defence.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was, Mr. Prosecutor, I believe the second day after -- after my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You mean, when you say your arrival, you mean your arrival in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before you arrived in The Hague, were you -- can you tell me when you were interviewed or spoken to by a representative of the Defence for Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was to make my statement which you have received, and that was perhaps a month or so prior to my coming here. I'm talking about my curriculum vitae and this statement of mine in connection with the expulsion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay, sir, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to be clear. I do not have a copy of that statement. So the first time that you were interviewed by the Defence was approximately one month ago? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I gave that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is the statement a written statement? Did it result in a written statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I did not. I just gave it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you review the statement, the written statement, after it was written? Or did you write it? Did you write the statement? Or did somebody else interview you and write the statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote that statement myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In that statement, did you write anywhere that you were put into home detention? Is that contained in the statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall at this point, because I wrote about it on a number of occasions. And given the limitations of space, I'm not quite sure whether I put it precisely in that way, but I believe that in the book I talked about it the most as -- the most important document. Perhaps I did not refer to it as house detention, or maybe I did refer to it in a pejorative sense, but I am not quite certain at this point. I considered the petition the most important of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And all the rest is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, let me tell you why I am putting this question to you. Because we did not receive your statement, we're not entitled to that under the Rules, but we did receive a summary of your testimony from the Defence, and contained in that summary it states that you would testify that all three officials were put into home detention. Now, is that something that you ever stated to the Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All three? Which officials?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is a reference in context to Jovan Raskovic, the witness, and the third person whose name escapes me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that something, sir, that you told the Defence counsel that you and Mr. Raskovic and the other gentleman were put into home detention?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the sense that we explained to Their Honours. Because you insisted on "house detention" as such, and we were in it, all of us, in a way, and all of us were in the same position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, the phrase "home detention" did not come from me. It came from the Defence counsel in their summary of your testimony. So I am asking if you, in fact, ever used that term when making your statement to the Defence. Did you in fact say that you and the other men were put into home detention? Did you say that, or not, sir? That seems like an important point that you could remember.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall right now whether I did put that in the statement, because I have -- my description of those events is in the books, the collection about Jovan Raskovic which gives these descriptions in detail, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, sorry. Mr. Witness I am not quite sure whether the books you keep referring to are part of the evidence here. If they are, I'm sorry. But if they are not, I don't think that's what is being asked. What is being asked is what you discussed in preparation for coming to this case. Let's distinguish between the books that you may have written and the preparations for coming to this case. Do you think you can do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you think you can do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please do that. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now that we're focused -- I am grateful, Your Honour. Now that we're focused on your preparation for this case, and you said that you wrote this statement just a month ago, can you tell us, did you say, in that statement, did you write in that statement that you and Mr. Raskovic and Mr. Dobrijevic were put into home detention, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I limited that statement to just myself, that I did not refer individually to each one of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, that is not really the import of the question. It is not who is referred to. The import of the question is: Did you say that you and the other men were put into home detention?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I did in that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that was not accurate, was it, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've told you that I'm not quite certain, but I think that I put that there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, sir, then why is it that when I was asking you the question earlier about home detention, you started saying you didn't know what that meant and what did I mean by that, when in fact you're now telling us that you used those very words in your statement one month ago?
